title: 22. Interview: Design URL Shortener (bit.ly / TinyURL)
summary: Interview Q&A for Design URL Shortener (bit.ly / TinyURL) — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Design URL Shortener (bit.ly / TinyURL) interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Step 6: Trade-offs & Interview Q&A (5 min)
sections.body:
### Trade-offs Discussed
- **301 vs 302** — 301 saves origin bandwidth but loses click visibility; 302 gives accurate counts at the cost of one extra hop. We pick 302 by default and offer 301 for premium links.
- **Snowflake vs DB auto-increment vs UUID** — Snowflake is sortable, ID generation is local (no DB round-trip), and IDs fit in 64 bits. Auto-increments create a single-writer bottleneck; UUIDs are long and unsortable.
- **DynamoDB vs sharded Postgres** — DynamoDB scales transparently with zero ops but is more expensive at steady state and locks you to AWS; sharded Postgres (Citus) is cheaper long-term but ops-heavy.
- **Sync analytics vs async** — Async via Kafka decouples the redirect path (must stay <50 ms) from the analytics path (can lag seconds). The trade-off is eventual consistency of stats and the operational cost of a streaming pipeline.
- **Custom-alias enforcement** — Relational unique constraint (simple, slow at huge scale) vs DynamoDB conditional write (scales, weaker secondary queries).

### Conceptual Interview Questions

### Q1. Why use base62 encoding for short codes instead of base64 or just hex?
**Answer:** Base62 uses `[0-9A-Za-z]` — 62 URL-safe characters — so the short code never needs percent-encoding and can be embedded in tweets, QR codes, or printed URLs without ambiguity. Base64 includes `+`, `/`, `=` which break in URLs unless percent-encoded; hex doubles the string length (16 chars vs 7). With 7 base62 chars we get 62⁷ ≈ 3.5 trillion combinations — enough for ~100 M new URLs/day for 95 years. The slight downside is the encoding table is non-standard, but it's a 62-byte lookup array.
**Visual:**
```
hex      7f3a9c1b            16 chars
base64   fTqcGw==             8 chars (with padding, has + / =)
base62   3F9aQ2               6-7 chars, URL-safe
```

### Q2. What's the difference between 301 and 302 redirects, and which should the shortener use?
**Answer:** 301 (Moved Permanently) tells browsers and crawlers to cache the redirect forever — great for origin bandwidth, terrible for analytics because subsequent clicks never reach us. 302 (Found) is non-permanent; the browser re-checks on every visit, letting us count every click and rotate destinations if needed. bit.ly historically used 301 for SEO link juice and 302 for analytics — a trade-off. Our default is 302 + `Cache-Control: max-age=300` at the CDN: the edge caches for 5 min (saving origin bandwidth) while the browser still pings us. We expose a per-link toggle for marketers who want 301 for SEO.
**Visual:**
```
301:  Browser --301+cached--> LongURL        (no further hits to us)
302:  Browser --302 (revalidate)--> Origin --> LongURL
                                   |
                              (count click)
```

### Q3. How does Snowflake ID generation avoid the single-point-of-failure of a DB sequence?
**Answer:** Snowflake generates IDs locally on each pod using `(timestamp << 22) | (machine_id << 10) | sequence`. Each pod has a unique `machine_id` assigned at boot (from ConfigMap / EC2 instance id), so two pods can never produce the same ID even if their timestamps and sequence numbers coincide. The only coordination needed is `machine_id` assignment, which is a one-time startup operation, not per-request. This removes the DB sequence bottleneck — Snowflake has been measured at 4 M IDs/s per pod in production at Twitter/X. Clock skew is the main risk; NTP keeps it < 1 ms, and the monotonic guard inside Snowflake prevents going backward.
**Visual:**
```
64-bit Snowflake ID
| 41 bits timestamp (ms since epoch) | 10 bits machine | 12 bits seq |
```

### Q4. Why cache-aside instead of write-through for the redirect cache?
**Answer:** Write-through populates the cache at write time, but in a URL shortener, writes are 100× rarer than reads and the long URL rarely changes after creation — so pre-populating the cache wastes memory on links that may never be clicked. Cache-aside loads lazily on first miss; only hot links end up cached, which matches the power-law distribution of clicks (top 1% of links = 80% of traffic). The downside is the first request after a cache miss is slower, but CDN edge caching smooths that out. We do pre-warm a small "trending" set every 5 min via a background job to absorb viral spikes.
**Visual:**
```
write-through:  Write --> Update DB AND Cache   (every link cached, mostly wasted)
cache-aside:    Write --> DB                    Read --> Cache miss? --> DB --> Cache
```

### Q5. How would you handle a viral link that suddenly spikes from 100 QPS to 50 000 QPS?
**Answer:** Three layers absorb the spike. (1) The CDN edge returns a cached 301 — typically 80% of requests never reach origin. (2) Redis cluster has 5-min TTLs on hot codes; with a 6-node Redis Cluster we serve 200 k QPS easily. (3) DynamoDB on-demand capacity scales instantly per-partition; a single hot partition can sustain 3 000 RCUs. To prevent the first miss from stampeding, we use request coalescing — within a 50 ms window, only one thread fetches from DynamoDB while others wait on a promise. Finally, a trending detector (Flink top-N over the last minute) pre-warms any code crossing 1 000 QPS, so the spike hits a warm cache.
**Visual:**
```
50k QPS spike
   |
   +--80% CDN (40k)   --> 301 cached, origin untouched
   +--18% Redis (9k)  --> hot cache, ms latency
   +--2% DynamoDB (1k)--> on-demand RCU scales
```

### Q6. How would you prevent abuse — spam, phishing, malware distribution through short links?
**Answer:** Defense in depth. (1) Rate limit `POST /shorten` per IP (token bucket in Redis) — 50/hour for anonymous, 1 000/hour for pro accounts. (2) Synchronous Safe Browsing API check on the long URL before accepting — rejects known phishing/malware. (3) Async ML classifier on URL features (length, entropy, TLD, age of domain) flags suspicious links for human review. (4) Periodic re-scan of all active links every 24 h via a Kafka job — a link that was clean at submission can be hijacked later. (5) Account-level abuse quota: a single account creating 10 000 links/day triggers review. (6) "Report this link" UI surface that feeds back into the training set.
**Visual:**
```
POST /shorten
  |
  +--> rate-limit (Redis token bucket)        -- 429 if exceeded
  +--> Safe Browsing API (sync, <50ms)        -- 403 if known bad
  +--> entropy/feature classifier (async)     -- flag for review
  +--> write mapping
  +--> enqueue re-scan job (24h TTL)
```

### Q7. Why use DynamoDB TTL for expiration instead of a cron job that deletes expired rows?
**Answer:** DynamoDB TTL is built-in: you set a `ttl_epoch` attribute and AWS deletes the item at no extra cost within 48 hours of the timestamp. A cron job would require scanning the table (expensive on a 183 B-row table), holding locks, and ops overhead. TTL also propagates to DynamoDB Streams, so we can emit a "link expired" event for cache invalidation and analytics. The trade-off is TTL deletion is not instantaneous — there can be a 48 h window where the row exists past `expires_at`. We close that gap by also checking `expires_at < now()` in the redirector-svc; if expired, we return 410 Gone and delete on read.
**Visual:**
```
expires_at=1700000000
  |
  +--> TTL attribute set
  +--> DynamoDB deletes within 48h (async, free)
  +--> redirector-svc ALSO checks expires_at < now() -> 410 Gone (instant)
```

### Scenario-Based Interview Questions

### Q1. A customer reports that their short link suddenly redirects to a 404 — how do you debug?
**Answer:** First, reproduce: `curl -i https://bit.ly/{code}` and inspect the response. If it's a 404 from our service, check (1) Redis cache — was it evicted prematurely? (2) DynamoDB — `aws dynamodb get-item` directly. If DynamoDB has the row, the issue is between cache and DB (stale negative cache from a 404 — check `negative_cache_ttl`). If DynamoDB returns nothing, check TTL: was the link expired? `expires_at` vs current time. If TTL deleted it, the customer set a TTL they forgot about, or a malicious actor deleted via the owner API (check audit log). If the 404 is coming from the *destination* long URL, the shortener is fine — tell the customer their site is down. End-to-end traceability: every redirect emits a click event with the resolution path (`cache_hit`/`db_hit`/`404`), so the dashboard should already show the anomaly.
**Visual:**
```
404 reported
  |
  +--> curl -i bit.ly/{code}
  |        |
  |        +-- 404 from us?  -> Redis -> DynamoDB -> TTL/audit
  |        +-- 404 from dest -> customer's site is down
```

### Q2. The CEO wants the shortener to support 1 B redirects/day (10× current). What changes?
**Answer:** Capacity check first: 1 B/day ≈ 11 600 QPS average, 60 000 QPS peak. The architecture already handles this with CDN absorbing 80% (≈ 48 k QPS at edge), Redis Cluster absorbing 18% (≈ 11 k QPS — needs ~30 Redis shards), and DynamoDB on-demand handling 2% (≈ 1.2 k QPS — trivial). Real bottlenecks: (1) Egress bandwidth at the API tier — 1 B × 1 KB = 1 TB/day egress; consider expanding CDN cache hit rate to 95%+ via longer TTLs. (2) Kafka throughput — 1 B events/day × 200 B = 200 GB/day; bump partitions from 24 to 96, RF=3, add Flink task slots. (3) ClickHouse ingest — use BufferMergeTree table to coalesce inserts. (4) Cost — DynamoDB on-demand at 1 B reads ≈ $250/day just for reads; consider Provisioned Capacity with autoscaling or migrate hot keys to Redis-only with DynamoDB as cold fallback.
**Visual:**
```
1B/day = 11.6k QPS avg, 60k peak
  | 80% CDN edge       (48k QPS) -- scale edge POPs
  | 18% Redis cluster  (11k QPS) -- ~30 shards
  | 2%  DynamoDB       (1.2k QPS) -- trivial
Kafka: 200 GB/day -> 96 partitions, RF=3
ClickHouse: BufferMergeTree for ingest
```

### Q3. A regional AWS outage takes down our primary DynamoDB region. What happens?
**Answer:** With DynamoDB Global Tables configured, the table is replicated to a standby region (e.g., us-east-1 → us-west-2 + eu-west-1). Route 53 health checks detect the primary region outage and re-route traffic to the standby region within ~60 seconds. During the failover window, reads may serve stale data for a few seconds (Global Tables is eventually consistent across regions), but no data is lost — Global Tables uses a last-writer-wins conflict resolution with vector clocks. Writes from the failed region that were queued in local application buffers are retried against the new primary. Post-incident: verify replication lag is back to < 1 s, run a chaos drill (`chaos stop-dynamodb-region`) to confirm the playbook. Without Global Tables, we'd have to fail over to a read replica (no writes) and reconcile via Kafka replay — a multi-hour RTO.
**Visual:**
```
us-east-1 (primary)  --repl-->  us-west-2 (standby)
   |  OUTAGE                   |
   v                           v
Route 53 detects    --60s-->  traffic to us-west-2
                            (writes ok, reads ok)
```

### Q4. Marketing runs a Super Bowl ad with a 6-character short URL; we expect 2 M clicks in 60 seconds. How do you prepare?
**Answer:** This is a classic flash-crowd scenario. Pre-warm: 1 h before kick-off, force-warm Redis and all CDN edge POPs for the code with `Cache-Control: max-age=300, s-maxage=600`. Use 301 (not 302) so browsers cache permanently — analytics is secondary for this one event. Provision DynamoDB at 50 k RCUs upfront (no autoscaling lag). Add Cloudflare Workers that can serve 301 directly from edge KV with zero origin dependency. Have the marketing team share the long URL with a tracking parameter on the *destination* page so they still get campaign attribution. Monitor in real time: Grafana dashboard with QPS, cache-hit ratio, error rate; SRE on-call with a runbook to flip DNS to a static S3-hosted page if the shortener melts. Post-event: drain Redis warm cache, scale down DynamoDB, archive the click log to S3 for marketing analytics.
**Visual:**
```
T-60m: warm CDN+Redis, set 301+s-maxage=600
T-0:   Super Bowl ad airs, 2M clicks / 60s = 33k QPS
       95% CDN edge -> 301 (no origin hit)
       5% origin -> Redis hit (pre-warmed)
T+5m:  cooldown, scale down, archive
```

### Q5. A security researcher finds that some 6-char codes are guessable — what went wrong and how do you fix it?
**Answer:** "Guessable" usually means the codes follow a predictable sequence — likely we used sequential auto-increment or a poorly-seeded PRNG. Sequential codes are an enumeration attack vector: an attacker can scrape every link ever created. Fix: switch to Snowflake IDs base62-encoded — they're sortable by time but the machine_id + sequence bits make adjacent codes non-adjacent in the encoded space. Even better, use a cryptographic permutation (Format-Preserving Encryption, FF1) over the Snowflake ID so the encoded code is computationally indistinguishable from random. Rotate: keep old sequential codes working (they're already out there) but only generate new codes via the new scheme. Add rate-limiting on `GET /{code}` returning 404 — more than 100 404s/minute per IP triggers a CAPTCHA. Audit: scan historical access logs for enumeration patterns.
**Visual:**
```
OLD (bad):   abc001, abc002, abc003 ... (scrapable)
NEW (good):  3F9aQ2, 7Xz2pL, K9bT4m ... (Snowflake + base62, non-adjacent)
BEST:        FF1(snowflake_id) -> looks random, still reversible
```

### Q6. Click analytics is lagging by 30 minutes — Kafka consumer lag is growing. What do you do?
**Answer:** First, find the bottleneck. Check Kafka consumer lag dashboard — is lag uniform across partitions (consumer too slow) or skewed (one partition has all the data, indicating a hot key)? If uniform: scale up consumer pods and increase `max.poll.records` and `fetch.max.bytes`. If skewed: hot key (a viral link dominates click events) — add a partitioner that hashes on `(code, minute_bucket)` to spread load. If Flink is the bottleneck: check backpressure, increase task slots, ensure checkpoint interval isn't too aggressive. Quick mitigation: increase ClickHouse batch interval from 5 s to 30 s (fewer inserts, less merge overhead). Long-term: pre-aggregate in Flink (top-N codes per minute) and write aggregates to ClickHouse; only raw events go to S3. If lag exceeds 1 h, page on-call — analytics staleness breaches the SLO.
**Visual:**
```
Kafka lag dashboard
  |
  +-- uniform lag? -> scale consumers, bump max.poll.records
  +-- skewed lag?  -> hot key -> hash partitioner (code, minute)
  +-- Flink backpressure? -> more task slots, longer checkpoint
  +-- ClickHouse too many parts? -> batch 30s, use Buffer engine
```

### Q7. A user complains their custom alias "my-brand" was reserved by someone else 5 minutes ago — how do we prevent squatting?
**Answer:** Three layers. (1) **Premium namespace reservation**: short, dictionary-word aliases (≤ 5 chars, common words) are gated behind verified accounts or paid plans — they can't be claimed by anonymous users. (2) **Abuse detection**: an account that reserves > 50 custom aliases/hour is flagged for review (squatting pattern). (3) **Dispute resolution**: a trademark-based takedown process (à la UDRP for domain names) where the verified trademark owner can claim an alias. For this specific user: check if "my-brand" was reserved by an anonymous account in the last hour — if so, flag for review and consider releasing if no legit use. If the reserver is a paying customer, offer the user an alternative ("my-brand-2") or initiate the trademark dispute flow. Long-term: reserve a block of common-brand aliases at startup, like the IANA reserved TLDs.
**Visual:**
```
POST /shorten {custom: "my-brand"}
  |
  +-- in reserved namespace? -> require verified+paid account
  +-- rate-limit per account: >50/hr -> flag
  +-- trademark DB match? -> block, route to dispute flow
  +-- else: reserve via Postgres unique constraint
```
